texto_desc: The server returned an HTTP 5xx response during normal testing activity, indicating an unhandled server-side error condition triggered by the request.
texto_impacto: Unhandled server errors can leak stack traces, internal paths, or framework details in the response body, and repeated triggering can degrade service stability.
texto_reco: Add centralized error handling that returns generic error responses to clients, log the underlying exception server-side only, and add regression tests for the input that triggered the error.

texto_desc: The application returns a verbose error message containing internal details such as stack traces, file paths, SQL fragments, or framework/library version information in its HTTP response.
texto_impacto: Attackers can use this leaked internal information to fingerprint the technology stack and craft more targeted exploits against known vulnerabilities.
texto_reco: Disable verbose/debug error output in production, return generic error pages to clients, and log detailed errors only to a secured server-side log.

texto_desc: The endpoint was found to accept an HTTP method (e.g. PUT, DELETE, TRACE, OPTIONS) beyond what is required for its documented functionality.
texto_impacto: Unnecessarily enabled HTTP methods expand the application's attack surface and may expose unintended functionality such as file upload/delete or debugging endpoints.
texto_reco: Restrict each endpoint to only the HTTP methods it legitimately requires, and explicitly reject or 405 any other method at the web server or framework level.

texto_desc: The set of HTTP methods advertised in the 'Allow' header of an OPTIONS response does not match the methods actually accepted by the endpoint when invoked directly.
texto_impacto: A mismatch between advertised and actual behavior indicates inconsistent access control configuration, and can mislead security tooling or hide unadvertised functionality from routine review.
texto_reco: Ensure the 'Allow' header accurately reflects the methods implemented and enforced by the endpoint, and remove or properly restrict any method that should not be exposed.

texto_desc: The server accepts the HTTP TRACE method and reflects the raw request, including headers, back in the response body (Cross-Site Tracing).
texto_impacto: An attacker able to induce a TRACE request from a victim's browser can read HTTP headers otherwise inaccessible to JavaScript, such as cookies marked HttpOnly, aiding session hijacking.
texto_reco: Disable the TRACE method on the web server and any intermediate proxies, since it is rarely required for legitimate application functionality.

texto_desc: The endpoint returned an HTTP 401/403 response, confirming that an authentication or authorization check is enforced for the tested request.
texto_impacto: This is an informational/positive finding indicating a control is present; it is recorded to support coverage evidence rather than to flag a weakness.
texto_reco: No remediation required; continue to verify that all sibling and newly added endpoints enforce the same authentication/authorization checks.

texto_desc: The request resulted in an HTTP redirect (3xx) response, and the destination was recorded for further analysis of redirect target handling.
texto_impacto: Uncontrolled redirect targets can be abused for phishing or open-redirect chaining if the destination is influenced by user-controlled input.
texto_reco: Verify that redirect destinations are drawn from a fixed, trusted set of URLs and that any user-influenced redirect parameter is validated against an allowlist.

texto_desc: Repeated or malformed requests sent during rate-limit testing caused the server to stop responding or return persistent errors, indicating a stability/availability failure under load.
texto_impacto: An attacker can intentionally trigger this condition to cause a denial of service, taking the application offline for all legitimate users.
texto_reco: Add input validation and resource limits (timeouts, request size caps, connection limits) so malformed or high-volume input cannot crash the service, and add monitoring/alerting for repeated failures.

texto_desc: The baseline request used to establish normal behavior before rate-limit testing was itself rejected with a 403 Forbidden response, preventing a valid comparison baseline.
texto_impacto: This is primarily a testing/coverage artifact; however, if legitimate baseline traffic is unexpectedly forbidden it may indicate an overly aggressive or misconfigured access control rule affecting real users.
texto_reco: Review the access control or WAF rule that produced the 403 response to confirm it is not blocking legitimate traffic, then re-run rate-limit testing once a valid baseline is available.

texto_desc: The endpoint accepted a burst of repeated identical or near-identical requests without applying any throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA challenge.
texto_impacto: Absence of rate limiting enables brute-force attacks against authentication and OTP endpoints, credential stuffing, resource exhaustion, and abuse of paid-per-call backend services (e.g. SMS/email providers).
texto_reco: Implement request throttling per user/IP/session/API key, add progressive lockout or CAPTCHA after repeated failures, and return HTTP 429 once the limit is exceeded.

texto_desc: The endpoint correctly enforced a rate limit, rejecting or throttling requests after a defined threshold was exceeded during testing.
texto_impacto: This is a positive/informational finding confirming a protective control is in place; it is recorded to document coverage rather than to flag a weakness.
texto_reco: No remediation required; periodically re-verify the rate limit threshold remains appropriate as usage patterns and endpoint criticality change.

texto_desc: A rate-limiting mechanism (e.g. HTTP 429 response, Retry-After header, or throttling delay) was detected on the endpoint during automated testing.
texto_impacto: This is an informational finding used to record the presence and behavior of a rate-limiting control for coverage purposes.
texto_reco: No remediation required; confirm the detected threshold and lockout duration align with the endpoint's sensitivity (e.g. tighter limits for authentication and OTP flows).

texto_desc: A JSON Web Token (JWT) used for authentication or session handling was observed being transmitted over an unencrypted HTTP connection.
texto_impacto: A network attacker performing man-in-the-middle interception can capture the token in transit and replay it to impersonate the legitimate user, since JWTs are typically bearer credentials.
texto_reco: Enforce HTTPS for all endpoints that transmit or accept JWTs, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and set the Secure flag on any cookie carrying a token.

texto_desc: The application does not return the HTTP Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) response header, so browsers are not instructed to enforce HTTPS-only connections for this host.
texto_impacto: Without HSTS, users who access the site over plain HTTP (e.g. via a bookmarked or typed HTTP link) remain exposed to SSL-stripping and man-in-the-middle downgrade attacks.
texto_reco: Add the 'Strict-Transport-Security' header with a suitably long max-age (e.g. 31536000) and includeSubDomains, and consider HSTS preload list submission once verified.

texto_desc: The JWT header does not include an 'alg' claim, or the claim could not be determined, leaving the signature algorithm used to verify the token ambiguous.
texto_impacto: Ambiguity in the signing algorithm can be leveraged in algorithm-confusion attacks if the server's verification logic trusts the algorithm declared in an attacker-supplied token.
texto_reco: Configure the JWT library to require and pin an explicit, expected signing algorithm on verification, rejecting tokens that omit or alter the 'alg' header.

texto_desc: The application accepts JWTs with the 'alg' header set to 'none', meaning the token's signature is not verified at all.
texto_impacto: An attacker can forge an arbitrary, unsigned token with any claims (including elevated privileges or another user's identity) and have it accepted as valid, resulting in full authentication bypass.
texto_reco: Explicitly reject tokens with 'alg: none' and configure the JWT verification library to enforce an allowlist of accepted signing algorithms, never inferring the algorithm from the token itself.

texto_desc: The JWT is signed with an HMAC-based algorithm (e.g. HS256) using a secret that is weak, short, or otherwise brute-forceable.
texto_impacto: An attacker who recovers or brute-forces the weak HMAC secret can forge arbitrary valid tokens, resulting in full authentication and authorization bypass.
texto_reco: Use a long, high-entropy, securely stored HMAC secret (or migrate to an asymmetric algorithm such as RS256/ES256), and rotate the secret if compromise is suspected.

texto_desc: The JWT is signed using an RSA-based asymmetric algorithm (e.g. RS256), which was recorded during signature-algorithm analysis.
texto_impacto: This is primarily an informational finding describing the signing scheme in use; risk depends on correct key management and algorithm pinning by the verifier.
texto_reco: Ensure the public key used for verification is fetched from a trusted, pinned source, and confirm the verifier does not accept algorithm-confusion attacks that swap RS256 for HS256 using the public key as an HMAC secret.

texto_desc: The JWT is signed using an ECDSA-based asymmetric algorithm (e.g. ES256), which was recorded during signature-algorithm analysis.
texto_impacto: This is primarily an informational finding describing the signing scheme in use; risk depends on correct key management, nonce handling, and algorithm pinning by the verifier.
texto_reco: Ensure the public key used for verification is fetched from a trusted, pinned source and that the ECDSA implementation uses properly random nonces to avoid private-key recovery attacks.

texto_desc: The JWT header contains an embedded 'jwk' (JSON Web Key) claim, allowing the token itself to supply the public key used to verify its own signature.
texto_impacto: If the verifier trusts the embedded key without validating it against a known, trusted key store, an attacker can self-sign a token with their own key pair and have it accepted as valid.
texto_reco: Ignore or reject the 'jwk' header claim during verification; always verify signatures against a server-side allowlist of trusted, pre-registered keys.

texto_desc: The JWT header contains a 'jku' (JWK Set URL) claim, allowing the token to point the verifier to an attacker-controllable URL to fetch the verification key.
texto_impacto: If the verifier fetches and trusts the key from an unvalidated 'jku' URL, an attacker can host their own key set and forge validly-signed tokens, resulting in authentication bypass; the fetch can also be abused for SSRF.
texto_reco: Ignore the 'jku' header or strictly validate it against an allowlist of trusted, pre-registered key-set URLs before fetching, and never resolve it to arbitrary attacker-supplied hosts.

texto_desc: The JWT header includes a 'kid' (Key ID) claim used to select which key to use for signature verification.
texto_impacto: If the 'kid' value is used unsafely (e.g. as a file path or SQL parameter, or without restricting it to a known key set) it can enable key-confusion, path traversal, or injection attacks against the verification logic.
texto_reco: Validate the 'kid' value strictly against an allowlist of known key identifiers server-side, and never use it directly to construct file paths or queries.

texto_desc: The JWT header contains an 'x5u' (X.509 URL) claim, allowing the token to direct the verifier to fetch a certificate chain from an attacker-controllable URL.
texto_impacto: If the verifier trusts a certificate fetched from an unvalidated 'x5u' URL, an attacker can supply a self-issued certificate and forge validly-signed tokens; the fetch can also be abused for SSRF.
texto_reco: Ignore the 'x5u' header or strictly validate it against an allowlist of trusted certificate URLs before fetching, and validate the full certificate chain against a trusted root CA.

texto_desc: The JWT header contains an 'x5c' (X.509 certificate chain) claim embedding the certificate used to verify the token's signature directly in the token.
texto_impacto: If the verifier trusts the embedded certificate without validating it against a trusted root CA and revocation status, an attacker can embed a self-signed certificate and forge validly-signed tokens.
texto_reco: Always validate the embedded certificate chain against a trusted, pinned root CA and check revocation status; never trust the leaf certificate's public key without full chain validation.

texto_desc: The JWT does not include an 'exp' (expiration time) claim, meaning the token has no defined validity period and remains usable indefinitely once issued.
texto_impacto: A token that never expires increases the impact of any token leak, since a stolen token remains valid for the attacker to replay indefinitely instead of only within a bounded window.
texto_reco: Always include a short-lived 'exp' claim on issued tokens and reject any token missing it during verification; pair with refresh tokens for longer sessions.

texto_desc: The JWT does not include an 'iat' (issued-at time) claim, making it harder to audit when the token was originally created or to reason about its age.
texto_impacto: Missing issuance timestamps reduce the ability to detect anomalously old tokens being replayed and complicate forensic analysis after a suspected compromise.
texto_reco: Include an 'iat' claim on all issued tokens and use it, alongside 'exp', to enforce maximum token age policies.

texto_desc: The JWT does not include an 'nbf' (not-before) claim, so the token is considered valid immediately upon issuance with no defined activation delay.
texto_impacto: For tokens intended to become valid only at a future time (e.g. scheduled access grants), the absence of 'nbf' means such time-based restrictions cannot be enforced.
texto_reco: Include an 'nbf' claim wherever a token should not be usable before a specific point in time, and ensure verification logic rejects tokens presented before that time.

texto_desc: The JWT does not include an 'aud' (audience) claim identifying the intended recipient service(s) of the token.
texto_impacto: Without an audience restriction, a token legitimately issued for one service could be replayed against a different service that shares the same signing key or trust relationship, enabling token confusion attacks.
texto_reco: Include an 'aud' claim identifying the intended service(s) and require the verifier to check that its own identifier is present in the token's audience before accepting it.

texto_desc: The JWT does not include an 'iss' (issuer) claim identifying the party that issued the token.
texto_impacto: Without an issuer claim, a verifier that trusts multiple signing sources cannot distinguish tokens issued by a trusted authority from those issued elsewhere, weakening trust validation.
texto_reco: Include an 'iss' claim identifying the token issuer and require the verifier to check it against an allowlist of trusted issuers.

texto_desc: The JWT does not include a 'jti' (JWT ID) claim, meaning individual tokens cannot be uniquely identified or explicitly revoked/denylisted.
texto_impacto: Without a unique token identifier, the application cannot support fine-grained revocation (e.g. logging a single stolen token out), so a leaked token remains valid until natural expiry.
texto_reco: Include a unique 'jti' claim on issued tokens and maintain a revocation/denylist store keyed on this value for sensitive sessions that require the ability to force logout.

texto_desc: A JWT payload was found to contain sensitive data (e.g. PII, internal identifiers, or secrets) in a claim, and JWTs are base64url-encoded rather than encrypted, so this data is trivially readable by anyone holding the token.
texto_impacto: Since JWT payloads are not confidential by default, embedding sensitive data exposes it to any party that can intercept or is otherwise given the token, including client-side JavaScript and browser storage.
texto_reco: Remove sensitive data from JWT claims and instead reference it via an opaque identifier resolved server-side, or use an encrypted token format (JWE) if sensitive data must be embedded.

texto_desc: A JWT payload contains a privilege/role/permission claim (e.g. 'role': 'admin', 'isAdmin': true) that, if attacker-controlled or forgeable, could grant elevated access.
texto_impacto: If the token's signature is not properly verified, or if the claim can be influenced during token issuance, an attacker may be able to escalate privileges by manipulating this claim, resulting in full authorization bypass.
texto_reco: Ensure privilege claims are set exclusively server-side at issuance based on authoritative data, are covered by strict signature verification on every request, and re-validate current privileges server-side rather than trusting the claim as a long-lived source of truth.

texto_desc: The HTTP response discloses specific version information about the server software, framework, or libraries in use (e.g. via a Server or X-Powered-By header).
texto_impacto: Disclosed version information helps an attacker quickly identify known vulnerabilities affecting that specific software version, accelerating reconnaissance and exploit selection.
texto_reco: Suppress or generalize version-revealing headers at the web server/framework level, and keep underlying software patched regardless of whether the banner is hidden.

texto_desc: A session token, API key, or other authentication credential was found exposed in an HTTP response header, URL, or body where it should not be disclosed.
texto_impacto: A leaked token can be captured by anyone with access to logs, browser history, referrer headers, or intercepted traffic, and used to hijack the associated session or account.
texto_reco: Remove tokens from URLs and non-essential headers, transmit credentials only via secure channels (POST body over HTTPS), and rotate any token confirmed to have been exposed.

texto_desc: The WWW-Authenticate response header discloses the authentication realm name, which may reveal internal naming conventions, application identifiers, or infrastructure details.
texto_impacto: Realm disclosure aids reconnaissance by revealing internal naming conventions or system identifiers, though it is not directly exploitable on its own.
texto_reco: Use a generic, non-identifying realm value in the WWW-Authenticate header rather than one that reveals internal system or application names.

texto_desc: The HTTP response discloses an internal/private IP address (e.g. RFC1918 range) in a header, error message, or body content.
texto_impacto: Knowledge of internal network addressing aids an attacker in mapping the internal network topology, which is valuable for planning lateral movement after an initial foothold.
texto_reco: Remove internal IP addresses from responses visible to external clients, and ensure error handlers do not echo internal networking details.

texto_desc: The HTTP response includes a debug-related header (e.g. X-Debug, X-Debug-Token) indicating that debug or diagnostic mode is enabled on a reachable environment.
texto_impacto: Debug mode often exposes verbose stack traces, internal variable state, or profiling data, giving an attacker significant insight into application internals and potential additional vulnerabilities.
texto_reco: Disable debug/diagnostic modes in any environment reachable by untrusted clients, and gate such headers behind environment-specific configuration that defaults to off in production.

texto_desc: A cookie is set without the 'Secure' attribute, meaning the browser will also transmit it over unencrypted HTTP connections.
texto_impacto: If a user ever accesses the site over HTTP (intentionally or via downgrade), the cookie can be intercepted in transit by a network attacker, potentially leading to session hijacking.
texto_reco: Set the 'Secure' attribute on all cookies, particularly session and authentication cookies, so they are only ever transmitted over HTTPS.

texto_desc: A cookie is set without the 'HttpOnly' attribute, making it accessible to client-side JavaScript via document.cookie.
texto_impacto: If a Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability exists anywhere on the site, the missing HttpOnly attribute allows the injected script to directly read and exfiltrate the cookie, enabling session hijacking.
texto_reco: Set the 'HttpOnly' attribute on all cookies that do not need to be read by client-side scripts, particularly session and authentication cookies.

texto_desc: A cookie is set without a 'SameSite' attribute (or with 'SameSite=None' where not required), leaving it eligible to be sent on cross-site requests.
texto_impacto: Cookies without adequate SameSite protection are more exposed to Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks, since the browser will attach them to requests originating from other sites.
texto_reco: Set 'SameSite=Lax' or 'SameSite=Strict' on session cookies as appropriate for the application's cross-site usage needs, reserving 'SameSite=None' (with Secure) only for cases that require cross-site delivery.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be a US Social Security Number (SSN) pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of SSNs constitutes a serious privacy breach that can facilitate identity theft, financial fraud, and regulatory non-compliance (e.g. state breach-notification laws).
texto_reco: Mask or remove SSNs from API responses and logs, apply field-level encryption at rest, and restrict access to full SSN values to only the specific workflows that legitimately require them.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be a UK National Insurance Number (NINO) pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of National Insurance Numbers can facilitate identity theft and benefit/tax fraud, and constitutes a personal data breach under UK GDPR.
texto_reco: Mask or remove NINOs from API responses and logs, apply field-level encryption at rest, and restrict access to only the workflows that legitimately require the full value.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be a Canadian Social Insurance Number (SIN) pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of SINs can facilitate identity theft and financial fraud, and constitutes a reportable personal information breach under Canadian privacy law.
texto_reco: Mask or remove SINs from API responses and logs, apply field-level encryption at rest, and restrict access to only the workflows that legitimately require the full value.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be a Brazilian CPF (Cadastro de Pessoas Físicas) number pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of CPF numbers can facilitate identity theft and fraud, and constitutes a personal data breach under Brazil's LGPD.
texto_reco: Mask or remove CPF numbers from API responses and logs, apply field-level encryption at rest, and restrict access to only the workflows that legitimately require the full value.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be a French NIR (numéro de sécurité sociale) pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of the NIR can facilitate identity theft and fraud, and constitutes a personal data breach under GDPR and French data protection law.
texto_reco: Mask or remove NIR values from API responses and logs, apply field-level encryption at rest, and restrict access to only the workflows that legitimately require the full value.

texto_desc: An HTTP header name or value suggests personally identifiable information is being transmitted in headers (e.g. a custom header carrying an email, full name, or national ID).
texto_impacto: Transmitting PII via headers increases the risk of it being captured in proxy, CDN, or access logs that were not designed to handle sensitive data, and bypasses body-level data protection controls.
texto_reco: Move PII out of headers and into the request/response body where it can be governed by existing data-handling and logging controls, or avoid transmitting it unless strictly necessary.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be a credit/payment card number (PAN) pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of full card numbers is a critical data breach with direct financial fraud implications and constitutes a serious PCI-DSS compliance violation.
texto_reco: Never return full PANs in API responses; mask all but the last four digits, ensure card data is tokenized/encrypted per PCI-DSS requirements, and audit all code paths that touch payment data.

texto_desc: The HTTP response contains what appears to be an International Bank Account Number (IBAN) pattern in the body or headers.
texto_impacto: Exposure of bank account numbers can facilitate financial fraud, unauthorized transactions, and social engineering attacks against the account holder.
texto_reco: Mask or remove IBAN values from API responses and logs, apply field-level encryption at rest, and restrict access to only the workflows that legitimately require the full value.

texto_desc: The HTTP response discloses internal backend implementation details, such as internal hostnames, service names, stack traces, or internal API paths.
texto_impacto: Backend implementation details help an attacker map the application's internal architecture, informing more targeted attacks against specific components.
texto_reco: Sanitize responses to remove internal implementation details before they reach external clients, and route errors through a generic external-facing handler.

texto_desc: The HTTP response discloses an internal domain name or hostname (e.g. *.internal, *.corp) not intended for external visibility.
texto_impacto: Internal domain names aid an attacker's reconnaissance of the organization's internal infrastructure and naming conventions, supporting further attacks such as targeted phishing or DNS-based pivoting.
texto_reco: Remove internal hostnames from responses reachable by external clients, and review DNS/CDN configuration to ensure internal names are not inadvertently exposed.

texto_desc: The application does not return a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) response header, leaving the browser without a defined policy restricting the sources of scripts, styles, and other resources.
texto_impacto: Absence of CSP removes a key defense-in-depth control against Cross-Site Scripting; if a script-injection flaw is later found, CSP would otherwise have limited its impact.
texto_reco: Define and deploy a Content-Security-Policy header restricting script, style, and resource sources to trusted origins, starting in report-only mode if needed to validate before enforcement.

texto_desc: The application does not return the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff response header.
texto_impacto: Without this header, older browsers may MIME-sniff response content and render it as an unintended content type (e.g. executing a file served as text/plain as HTML/JS), increasing exposure to content-sniffing based attacks.
texto_reco: Add the 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' header to all HTTP responses to prevent browsers from MIME-sniffing away from the declared Content-Type.

texto_desc: The application does not return an X-Frame-Options header (or equivalent frame-ancestors CSP directive), leaving pages able to be embedded in a frame on another site.
texto_impacto: Absence of frame protection leaves the application exposed to clickjacking, where an attacker overlays the page in an invisible iframe to trick users into performing unintended actions.
texto_reco: Add an 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' or 'SAMEORIGIN' header, or a CSP 'frame-ancestors' directive, to prevent the page from being framed by untrusted origins.

texto_desc: The application does not return a Referrer-Policy response header, leaving the browser's default (often permissive) referrer-sharing behavior in effect.
texto_impacto: Without an explicit policy, full URLs (potentially including sensitive query parameters or tokens) may be leaked to third-party sites via the Referer header when users follow outbound links.
texto_reco: Add a 'Referrer-Policy' header (e.g. 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or stricter) to control how much referrer information is shared with other origins.

texto_desc: The application does not return a Permissions-Policy response header, leaving browser feature access (camera, microphone, geolocation, etc.) governed only by default browser behavior.
texto_impacto: Without an explicit Permissions-Policy, embedded third-party content or a compromised page component could gain access to sensitive browser features that the application does not itself need.
texto_reco: Add a 'Permissions-Policy' header that explicitly disables browser features not required by the application, following a least-privilege approach.

texto_desc: The application does not correctly validate one or more input parameters, accepting values outside the expected type, format, length, or range.
texto_impacto: Missing input validation is a root-cause weakness that commonly enables downstream issues such as injection, business-logic bypass, or application errors, depending on how the unvalidated value is subsequently used.
texto_reco: Apply strict, allowlist-based server-side validation (type, format, length, and range) to every input parameter, rejecting any value that does not conform, regardless of client-side checks already in place.

texto_desc: A time-based blind SQL injection payload (e.g. a database SLEEP/WAITFOR call) was injected into a parameter, and the response exhibited a delay consistent with the injected value, confirming the input reaches a SQL query unsanitized.
texto_impacto: An attacker can use time-based blind techniques to extract data from the database row by row without relying on visible error messages, and depending on database privileges may be able to read, modify, or delete data, or achieve full database compromise.
texto_reco: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database access; never build SQL via string concatenation with user input. Apply strict input validation as defense in depth.

texto_desc: A Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) payload injected into a parameter was reflected or stored and rendered by the application without adequate output encoding, indicating the browser would execute attacker-supplied script.
texto_impacto: An attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of a victim's session, enabling session/cookie theft, credential harvesting via fake login prompts, defacement, or actions performed on the victim's behalf.
texto_reco: Contextually encode all user-controlled output before rendering (HTML, attribute, JS, and URL encoding as appropriate), adopt a templating engine with auto-escaping, and deploy a restrictive Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.

texto_desc: A path traversal payload (e.g. '../' sequences or an absolute path) injected into a file-related parameter caused the application to access a file outside the intended directory.
texto_impacto: An attacker may be able to read arbitrary files from the server's filesystem, including application source code, configuration files, or credentials, and in some configurations write or overwrite files.
texto_reco: Validate user-supplied file references against a strict allowlist rather than sanitizing traversal sequences, resolve and canonicalize paths before use, and enforce that the resolved path remains within an intended base directory (chroot/jail where possible).

texto_desc: A NoSQL injection payload (e.g. MongoDB operator injection such as $ne, $gt, or a JavaScript expression) was injected into a parameter and altered the application's query logic or response.
texto_impacto: An attacker may be able to bypass authentication, extract or manipulate data beyond their authorization, or in some NoSQL engines achieve server-side code execution.
texto_reco: Use parameterized/typed query builders rather than concatenating raw user input into queries, strictly type and validate input (reject objects/operators where a scalar is expected), and apply least-privilege database accounts.

texto_desc: A format-string style payload (e.g. '%s', '%x', or similar specifiers) injected into a parameter produced anomalous application behavior or output, suggesting user input reaches a format-string function unsanitized.
texto_impacto: Depending on the underlying language/runtime, format-string injection can leak memory contents, cause a crash (denial of service), or in unmanaged languages potentially lead to code execution.
texto_reco: Never pass user-controlled input directly as a format string; always use it as an argument to a fixed format string, and validate/sanitize input that influences formatting behavior.

texto_desc: A Unicode-based payload (e.g. homoglyphs, normalization edge cases, or overlong encodings) injected into a parameter bypassed input filtering or caused inconsistent handling between validation and processing stages.
texto_impacto: Unicode normalization inconsistencies can be used to bypass input filters and validation logic (filter evasion), potentially enabling injection or authentication-bypass attacks that would otherwise be blocked.
texto_reco: Normalize all input to a single canonical Unicode form (e.g. NFC) before validation and again before use, and perform validation after normalization rather than before.

texto_desc: An OS command injection payload (e.g. shell metacharacters chained to a benign value) injected into a parameter caused the application to execute an attacker-influenced operating system command.
texto_impacto: Successful OS command injection typically leads to full remote code execution on the host, allowing the attacker to read/modify data, pivot to internal systems, or fully compromise the server.
texto_reco: Avoid invoking OS shell commands with user input entirely where possible; if unavoidable, use parameterized APIs (e.g. execve-style argument arrays) instead of shell string concatenation, and strictly allowlist input.

texto_desc: A Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) payload (e.g. a template expression like {{7*7}}) injected into a parameter was evaluated by the server's template engine, as shown by the computed result appearing in the response.
texto_impacto: SSTI frequently escalates to full remote code execution, since many template engines expose the underlying language runtime, allowing an attacker to read files, exfiltrate data, or execute arbitrary commands on the server.
texto_reco: Never render user-controlled input as a template; treat all user input strictly as data passed into a template's variables rather than as template code. Use a sandboxed or logic-less templating engine where user content must be processed.

texto_desc: A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) payload (a URL or hostname pointing to an internal/attacker-controlled resource) injected into a parameter caused the server to make an outbound request to that target.
texto_impacto: An attacker can use the vulnerable server as a proxy to reach internal-only resources (metadata services, internal admin panels, databases) that are not directly reachable from the internet, potentially leading to credential theft or further compromise.
texto_reco: Validate and allowlist destination hosts/URLs for any server-initiated outbound request, block requests to private/internal IP ranges and cloud metadata endpoints, and disable unnecessary URL-fetching functionality.

texto_desc: The same parameter name was supplied multiple times in a single request (HTTP Parameter Pollution), and the application processed it in an unexpected or inconsistent way (e.g. using the first, last, or a concatenated value, differently across components).
texto_impacto: Inconsistent handling of duplicate parameters between the application, WAF, and any upstream/downstream components can be abused to bypass validation performed by one layer while a different value is processed by another.
texto_reco: Explicitly define and enforce how duplicate parameters are handled at every layer that parses the request, reject requests containing unexpected duplicate parameters, and ensure WAF and application parameter parsing behavior are consistent.

texto_desc: Raw/malformed byte sequences (e.g. null bytes, control characters, or invalid encodings) injected into a parameter caused anomalous application behavior, indicating insufficient sanitization of non-standard byte input.
texto_impacto: Malformed byte input can be used to bypass string-based validation filters (e.g. null-byte truncation of a filename check), cause parsing errors, or in some cases trigger memory-safety issues in native components.
texto_reco: Validate and reject input containing null bytes or invalid encodings before further processing, and use safe, well-tested parsing libraries rather than manual byte-level string handling.

texto_desc: Submitting an array where the application expects a scalar value for a parameter (or vice versa) caused unexpected behavior, an error, or a change in application logic, indicating the parameter type is not validated server-side.
texto_impacto: Type confusion can be used to bypass validation logic that only checks scalar values, potentially altering query behavior (e.g. in NoSQL/ORM contexts) or causing denial of service via unhandled type errors.
texto_reco: Strictly enforce expected parameter types server-side (reject arrays/objects where a scalar is expected and vice versa) using schema validation before the value reaches business logic.

texto_desc: Manual testing confirmed that attacker-supplied input is reflected in the HTTP response and rendered by the browser without adequate output encoding, resulting in Cross-Site Scripting.
texto_impacto: An attacker can craft a malicious link containing the payload and, once a victim visits it, execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's session context, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, or unauthorized actions on the victim's behalf.
texto_reco: Contextually encode all reflected user input before rendering (HTML, attribute, JS, and URL encoding as appropriate), adopt output-encoding by default via the templating engine, and deploy a restrictive Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.
